newsitem.title: SPAIN: Iberian bonds to shine at short end in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Iberian bonds to shine at short end in 1997.

text.p: Having benefitted from European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) convergence this year, Iberian bonds should extend gains in 1997 versus core markets.
But the meat left is mostly at the short-end of the market, analysts said.

A possible turnaround in the world interest rate cycle next year should affect only marginally bond markets in both Spain and Portugal, which will likely be little changed at the long end. The spread over Germany at the other end should continue to narrow.

"We expect the (Spanish 10-year) spread over Bunds to move between 80 and 120 basis points (from the current 120 bps), while at the short end the fall could be up to 250 bp," said Valentin Fernandez, analyst at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
This should result in a steepening of the yield curve.

"In 1996 we saw a flattening of the yield curve, with a reduction in the differential between the two and 10-year (area). We expect it to widen toward 200 basis points," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist with Bank of America in Madrid.
He said he expects a very aggressive easing policy by the Bank of Spain next year, with the key money market rate at 4.5 percent by year-end from the current 6.25 percent.
Spain's official interest rate started 1996 at nine percent.
The downtrend in short-term rates should be even stronger in Portugal.

"I don't expect Spain's key money market rate to decline more than 50 basis point from the current 6.25 percent level, but in Portugal where the central bank is lagging behind, there's more room," said Luis Alzola, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.
He forecast Portugal's key money rate to decline around 90 basis points to around 6.0 percent by the end of 1997.
In the longer end of the curve, dealers have already made good use of the market trend.
"1997 is not going to be a year as easy as this one, when we had just to sit on our investment to make profits with bonds," said Joa Ermida, chief dealer with Santander in Lisbon.

"The market has already seen most of the gains we expected," said Mario Dias Vigario at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Lisbon. He expects the 10-year spread between bonos and Bunds to decline toward 110 at a three-year horizon, and then to 90 basis points.

On Thursday the 10-year spread between bonos and Bunds was trading at around 112 basis points, after hitting a record low at 104 bps last Monday. It has narrowed from 330 basis points at the start of March and from 500 in summer 1995.
The two values for Portugal were around 470 bps in the summer 1995, and around 270 in March 1996.
But analysts expect the Portuguese market to outperform.
Deutsche's Vigario expect the long-term yield to trade between 25 and 40 basis points under that of Spain, compared with a gap of four to five basis points in 10-year bonds now.

Within so-called "Club Med" countries, markets rate eastern countries over their western counterparts, with long-term interest rates currently lower in Portugal than in Spain, and lower in Spain than in Italy.

"Portuguese fundamentals are better than in Spain and Spanish ones outstrip Italy's," said Fernandez, who expects the 10-year spread between the two Iberian countries to move from zero to minus 20 basis points.
